newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels still insist Berisha resigns.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels still insist Berisha resigns.

text.p: Rebels holding key southern Albanian towns repeated on Saturday that President Sali Berisha must quit if order is to be restored to the country.

Agim Gozhita, a former army general who heads the rebel council in this key southern stronghold, said he had delivered that message to European officials and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino when they met on an Italian warship on Friday.
He told Reuters Television: "We accept the government of Fino. We made it clear, we want Berisha's resignation and we will give in our weapons when he does."
Gozhita said that those who had joined in the popular uprising over the past two weeks, whether in the north or south of the tiny Balkan country, all felt the same.

He stressed the motive for the rebellion was the loss of millions of dollars by thousands of Albanians when a string of fraudulent investment schemes collapsed in January and the deep suspicion that the then-ruling right-wing Democrats profited.
"We have told Fino that the government is to give the people back their money and suspend the accounts of the party members of Berisha's Democratic Party," he said.
Berisha's Democrats won general elections last year, widely viewed as deeply flawed. Berisha was elected to a new five-year term by parliament early this month.
He named Fino, an opposition Socialist, prime minister last week in a desperate bid to regain control of his country, which has been swept by anarchy for the past two weeks.
Asked if foreign troops were required to sort out the chaos in Albania, he said: "We recognise there is a problem but we hope Fino will work it out without the help of foreign troops."
Thousands of self-styled rebels are now heavily armed in the south, having looted army arsenals throughout the region. Armed gangs, operating as outlaws, are also roaming the region.
In Gjirokaster on Friday, gunmen rammed a captured tank into the state savings bank and hauled a safe through the streets.
In the nearby port of Sarande, gunmen blew a hole in another bank on Saturday and made off with the safe and an undisclosed amount of cash.
Albanian refugees have begun to flee across the Adriatic Sea to Italy but so far there has been no mass movement towards the long Greek border with Albania, as there was in 1991.
The Greek border has been the scene of desperate families trying to cross and often being separated because some members had legal visas and others did not.
Vassilis Ioannis, who had a visa, was stopped from crossing on Friday with his wife and two children because they did not have legal documents.
Ioannis said tearfully the family did not know where to go, they did not want to turn back for fear they could be killed on the road by armed outlaw gangs.
"Where can we go with the children? What can we do, go back so they can kill us?" he asked. "I have no money. What about the children? What will we do with them?"
His wife threw herself on the car of a Greek border guard, pleading for understanding but was hauled away.
Greek security has been heightened along the border after rebels took over both main Albanian border posts and rampaged along the frontier.
Greece, with some 350,000 Albanians residing in the country -- mostly illegal workers -- has accepted Albanians with legal visas but is keeping out illegal immigrants.
Three Greek navy ships evacuated several hundred foreigners -- including Chinese, Jordanians and Egyptians -- from the Albanian port of Durres on Saturday to the island of Corfu.
